content: 1. Infants who struggle with cup feeding may exhibit behaviors such as difficulty managing the cup, spilling a significant amount of milk, appearing unsatisfied, or taking an extended time to complete feeding. In one study, 7% of infants (1 out of 152) were provided with cup feeds. 2. In the study conducted by Yilmaz et al., 10% of infants in the cup-feeding group (26 out of 254) and 8% in the bottle-feeding group (21 out of 268) were excluded due to non-compliance with the feeding protocol. 3. Schubiger et al. reported that 11% of infants in the cupor spoon-feeding group (28 out of 250) violated the protocol. Among these, 19 mothers requested bottle feeding, and 9 infants were reported to have failed with spoon or cup feeding. 4. A review of the literature on the acceptability of avoiding feeding bottles and teats among healthcare personnel identified 10 studies conducted in five countries (Canada, Germany, India, the United Kingdom, and the United States). Healthcare workers expressed a general dislike for cup feeding and showed ambivalence toward bottle feeding. 5. Some healthcare providers believed that the method of feeding does not significantly impact the infant and, in some cases, suggested that bottle feeding might be preferable. Bottles were described by some as essential or even beneficial, particularly when mothers faced challenges with breastfeeding. 6. In neonatal intensive care units, bottles were often considered necessary due to the prioritization of medical care over breastfeeding. Many studies indicated that healthcare providers preferred bottles over other feeding methods, such as cup feeding, with moderate confidence in the evidence. 7. Implementing the avoidance of feeding bottles and teats may involve resource challenges, such as the time required for healthcare workers to teach and support mothers in using alternative feeding methods like cups, as well as the need for adequate staff capacity and training. 8. Recommendations suggest that if expressed breast milk or other feeds are medically indicated for term infants, feeding methods such as cups, spoons, or bottles and teats may be used during their stay at the facility, based on moderate-quality evidence. 9. Mothers should be discouraged from providing any food or fluids other than breast milk unless medically indicated. They should also be supported in recognizing and responding to their infants’ feeding cues, fostering closeness and comfort during their stay in maternity and newborn care facilities. 10. For preterm infants unable to breastfeed directly, non-nutritive sucking and oral stimulation may be beneficial until breastfeeding is established, though the evidence supporting this is of low quality. 11. Avoiding the use of feeding bottles and teats among preterm infants when additional feeds are medically indicated increases the likelihood of exclusive breastfeeding up to six months after discharge. 12. Many mothers value the convenience of pacifiers and feeding bottles, even when discouraged from using them. Mothers should be supported in making informed decisions about their use, with awareness of the slight risk of interference with breastfeeding during the early days. 13. Facilities providing maternity and newborn services should have a clearly written breastfeeding policy that is routinely communicated to staff and parents. However, the overall quality of evidence supporting this recommendation is very low. 14. Training healthcare workers on breastfeeding tends to improve their knowledge and compliance with breastfeeding initiatives, such as the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative. However, the evidence on its effect on attitudes and breastfeeding outcomes is inconsistent and of very low quality. 15. Antenatal breastfeeding education for mothers has been shown to have a moderate impact on breastfeeding duration. However, there is likely no significant difference in breastfeeding rates at three and six months between mothers who received antenatal education and those who did not. 16. Some studies reported fewer breastfeeding complications, such as nipple pain and trauma, among mothers who received guidance on proper positioning and attachment from lactation consultants. However, other studies found no significant differences in breastfeeding problems between groups. 17. Mothers value antenatal education on breastfeeding, and such education can help reduce complications and improve breastfeeding outcomes. However, the quality of evidence supporting these findings is moderate. 18. Healthcare facilities and staff should not promote breast-milk substitutes, feeding bottles, teats, or pacifiers in any part of the facility. Staff should also avoid providing these products to breastfeeding infants, in line with the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes. 19. Supporting mothers to respond to their infants’ behavioral cues for feeding, comfort, or closeness helps build nurturing relationships, increases maternal confidence, and supports breastfeeding success. Methods to respond include breastfeeding, skin-to-skin contact, cuddling, carrying, talking, and singing. 20. Creating an enabling environment for breastfeeding involves systematic reviews and evidence synthesis to guide recommendations. This includes addressing resource implications, feasibility, equity, and human rights issues for each intervention. 21. Training healthcare workers on breastfeeding requires resources such as staff training costs, time, retention, capacity, and effective communication. Despite interest, breastfeeding training is often deprioritized compared to other maternal care training. 22. Health-facility staff providing infant feeding services should have sufficient knowledge, competence, and skills to support women in breastfeeding, though the evidence supporting this recommendation is of very low quality.
